questions: OpenShift architecture
F1
Red Hat OpenShift
Which OpenShift node role runs the Kubernetes API server, etcd, scheduler and controller managers?
Control plane (master) nodes
Worker (compute) nodes
Infrastructure nodes only
Bootstrap node permanently
Control plane nodes host the API server, etcd (cluster state), the scheduler and the controller managers. Production clusters use three control plane nodes for etcd quorum.
Correct: control plane nodes run the cluster's management components.
Wrong: worker nodes run application workloads.
Wrong: infra nodes host routers, registry and monitoring, not etcd.
Wrong: the bootstrap node is temporary and used only during installation.
A production cluster has 3 control plane nodes spread across 3 zones so losing one keeps etcd quorum.
Three control plane nodes give quorum; odd numbers avoid split-brain.
OpenShift architecture
F1
Red Hat OpenShift
Where should CP4I capability workloads such as queue managers and integration runtimes normally run?
On worker (compute) nodes
On control plane nodes alongside etcd
On the bootstrap node
On the load balancer appliance
Application workloads run on worker nodes. Control plane nodes are reserved for cluster management so that application load cannot starve etcd or the API server.
Correct: workloads belong on worker nodes.
Wrong: scheduling workloads on masters risks cluster stability.
Wrong: the bootstrap node does not exist after install.
Wrong: load balancers do not run pods.
A sizing plan dedicates 6 worker nodes to CP4I and keeps 3 control plane nodes unschedulable.
Exceptions such as compact 3-node clusters exist, but production best practice separates roles.
OpenShift architecture
F1
Kubernetes
What is etcd's role in an OpenShift cluster?
A distributed key-value store that holds the cluster's state and configuration
A container runtime
A load balancer
A metrics database for applications
etcd stores all Kubernetes objects (deployments, secrets, CRs). It is critical, so it must be backed up regularly and run with quorum.
Correct: etcd is the cluster state store.
Wrong: CRI-O is the container runtime.
Wrong: routers or external load balancers balance traffic.
Wrong: Prometheus stores metrics.
The platform team takes daily etcd backups as part of cluster disaster recovery.
Losing etcd quorum makes the API read-only or unavailable, so protect it.
OpenShift architecture
F2
Red Hat OpenShift
What is the purpose of OpenShift infrastructure nodes?
Hosting platform services such as the ingress router, internal image registry, monitoring and logging, separate from application workloads
Running etcd exclusively
Running only CP4I operators
Providing persistent storage hardware

Infra nodes isolate platform components (routers, registry, monitoring, logging) from application workloads. This improves stability, and under Red Hat subscription terms infra-only nodes may not need OpenShift subscriptions.
Correct: infra nodes run platform services.
Wrong: etcd runs on control plane nodes.
Wrong: operators are normal workloads.
Wrong: storage can be on any nodes or external.
Ingress routers on dedicated infra nodes keep a noisy integration workload from affecting routing.
Infra nodes are an isolation and cost pattern, not a storage role.
Kubernetes fundamentals
F1
Kubernetes
What is a Kubernetes Pod?
The smallest deployable unit, containing one or more containers that share network and storage
A physical server
A cluster of nodes
A storage class
A Pod groups containers that share an IP address, ports and volumes. Controllers such as Deployments and StatefulSets manage pods.
Correct: the pod is the smallest deployable unit.
Wrong: servers are nodes.
Wrong: a cluster is many nodes.
Wrong: a StorageClass defines provisioning.
An ACE integration runtime pod contains the runtime container (and possibly sidecars) sharing one network namespace.
Pod = shared network and storage context for containers.
Kubernetes fundamentals
F1
Kubernetes
Which controller is used for stateful workloads that need stable network identities and persistent storage per replica, such as Kafka brokers or MQ Native HA pods?
StatefulSet
Deployment
DaemonSet
Job
StatefulSets give each replica a stable identity (pod-0, pod-1, ...) and its own PVC through volumeClaimTemplates, which stateful systems require.
Correct: StatefulSets suit stateful replicas.
Wrong: Deployments treat replicas as interchangeable and stateless.
Wrong: DaemonSets run one pod per node.
Wrong: Jobs run to completion.
Kafka broker my-es-kafka-0 always reattaches to its own PVC after rescheduling.
Stable identity plus per-replica storage = StatefulSet.
Kubernetes fundamentals
F1
Kubernetes
Which Kubernetes object provides a stable virtual IP and DNS name for a set of pods selected by labels?
Service
ConfigMap
PersistentVolume
Secret
A Service selects pods by label and provides a stable ClusterIP and DNS name, load-balancing across ready endpoints.
Correct: Services give stable access to pods.
Wrong: ConfigMaps hold configuration.
Wrong: PVs are storage.
Wrong: Secrets hold sensitive data.
Applications connect to qm1-ibm-mq.cp4i.svc:1414 rather than to individual pod IPs.
Pods come and go; Services stay stable.
Kubernetes fundamentals
S2
Kubernetes
A Deployment has 3 replicas, but the Service sends no traffic to one pod. The pod is Running but not Ready. Why?
The pod's readiness probe is failing, so it is removed from the Service endpoints
The Service only supports two pods
The pod's liveness probe is passing
The node is a control plane node
Only pods whose readiness probe succeeds are added to Service endpoints. A Running but not Ready pod receives no traffic until it passes readiness.
Correct: failing readiness excludes the pod from endpoints.
Wrong: Services support many pods.
Wrong: a passing liveness probe would not exclude it.
Wrong: node role is not the reason.
An integration runtime is not Ready until its flows are deployed, so it receives no traffic during startup.
Readiness = receive traffic. Liveness = restart if unhealthy. Startup = allow slow starts.
Kubernetes fundamentals
T2
Kubernetes
A pod repeatedly restarts with status CrashLoopBackOff. Which command gives the MOST direct evidence of the cause?
oc logs <pod> --previous to see the logs of the last failed container, plus oc describe pod for events
oc get nodes
oc whoami
oc get storageclass
--previous shows the logs of the crashed container instance, and describe shows events such as OOMKilled, failed probes or missing mounts. Together they usually identify the root cause.
Correct: previous logs and events show why the container exits.
Wrong: node status is too general.
Wrong: shows only your identity.
Wrong: storage classes are unrelated unless mounts fail.
oc logs --previous reveals 'Error: unable to read server.conf.yaml', caused by a malformed configuration object.
CrashLoopBackOff: logs --previous, then describe for events and lastState.
Kubernetes fundamentals
T3
Kubernetes
A Kafka broker pod's lastState shows 'OOMKilled' (exit code 137). What is the MOST appropriate action?
Increase the container memory limit and align the JVM heap so heap plus off-heap usage fits within the limit, based on observed usage
Increase CPU requests only
Delete the topic
Lower the replication factor to 1

OOMKilled means the container exceeded its memory limit. For JVM workloads, the heap (-Xmx) plus off-heap memory (direct buffers, metaspace, page cache demands within the cgroup) must fit inside the limit with headroom.
Correct: adjust the memory limit and JVM sizing together.
Wrong: CPU does not prevent OOM.
Wrong: data loss and not the cause.
Wrong: reduces resilience without fixing memory.
Raising the broker limit from 4Gi to 8Gi while keeping -Xmx at 4g stopped the kills.
Exit code 137 / OOMKilled -> a memory limit problem, not CPU.
Namespaces and scope
F1
Kubernetes
Which of these Kubernetes resources is cluster-scoped rather than namespaced?
CustomResourceDefinition (CRD)
Deployment
ConfigMap
Secret
CRDs, Nodes, PersistentVolumes, StorageClasses, ClusterRoles and Namespaces are cluster-scoped. Deployments, ConfigMaps, Secrets and PVCs are namespaced.
Correct: CRDs are cluster-scoped.
Wrong: Deployments are namespaced.
Wrong: ConfigMaps are namespaced.
Wrong: Secrets are namespaced.
Two teams cannot run conflicting MQ operator versions that need different CRD versions in one cluster, because the CRD is shared.
Cluster-scoped resources are shared, so they constrain multi-tenancy.
Namespaces and scope
F2
Kubernetes
Which TWO of the following are namespaced resources? (Select TWO.)
PersistentVolumeClaim
PersistentVolume
RoleBinding
StorageClass
PVCs and RoleBindings belong to a namespace. PVs, StorageClasses and ClusterRoleBindings are cluster-scoped.
Correct: PVCs are namespaced.
Wrong: PVs are cluster-scoped.
Correct: RoleBindings are namespaced.
Wrong: StorageClasses are cluster-scoped.
A queue manager's PVC sits in cp4i-prod and binds to a cluster-scoped PV.
PVC (namespaced) binds to PV (cluster-scoped).
Namespaces and scope
S2
Kubernetes
Which mechanism limits the total CPU and memory that all pods in a team's namespace can request?
ResourceQuota
LimitRange alone
NetworkPolicy
PodDisruptionBudget
ResourceQuota caps aggregate resource consumption per namespace (requests, limits, object counts). LimitRange sets per-container defaults and min/max values.
Correct: ResourceQuota caps namespace totals.
Wrong: LimitRange is per pod or container, not aggregate.
Wrong: NetworkPolicy controls traffic.
Wrong: PDBs control voluntary disruptions.
cp4i-dev-teamA has a quota of 16 CPU and 64Gi requests.
Quota = total. LimitRange = per-object defaults and bounds.
Namespaces and scope
T2
Kubernetes
Creating a new integration runtime fails with 'exceeded quota: compute-resources, requested: limits.cpu=2, used: 15, limited: 16'. What should be done?
Increase the namespace quota, reduce other workloads' limits, or reduce the new runtime's CPU limit
Delete the cert-manager namespace
Change the storage class
Restart etcd
The ResourceQuota blocks the pod because the new limits would exceed the namespace total. Adjust the quota or the resource settings.
Correct: quota and resource settings need adjusting.
Wrong: unrelated and harmful.
Wrong: storage does not affect CPU quota.
Wrong: dangerous and unrelated.
Scaling down an idle test runtime frees 2 CPU of quota.
Quota errors appear at admission time on the ReplicaSet or StatefulSet events.
Namespaces and scope
D3
Red Hat OpenShift
A platform must host 20 integration teams on one cluster with fair resource sharing and isolation. Which combination is MOST effective?
One namespace per team with ResourceQuota, LimitRange, RBAC, NetworkPolicies, and optionally dedicated node pools for sensitive teams
All teams in one namespace with shared admin
One cluster per developer
No quotas, to maximize flexibility
Namespaces with quotas, limits, RBAC and network policies are the standard soft multi-tenancy toolkit. Node pools (labels and taints) add stronger isolation where needed.
Correct: the full namespace-based tenancy toolkit.
Wrong: no isolation or accountability.
Wrong: excessive cost and sprawl.
Wrong: noisy neighbours could starve others.
The payments team gets its own tainted node pool; other teams share general workers under quotas.
Soft multi-tenancy = namespace + quota + RBAC + NetworkPolicy.
Environment topology
S2
Red Hat OpenShift
A company has development, test, UAT and production environments for CP4I. Which topology is MOST commonly recommended?
At least separate production from non-production clusters; non-production environments can share a cluster in separate namespaces
All environments in one namespace
Production and development in the same namespace
A separate cluster for every developer

Separating production clusters protects them from non-production change, including cluster-scoped operator and CRD upgrades. Non-production environments often share a cluster, separated by namespaces, for cost efficiency.
Correct: production is isolated; non-production is shared by namespace.
Wrong: no isolation at all.
Wrong: production must be separate.
Wrong: excessive cost.
Cluster A hosts cp4i-dev, cp4i-test and cp4i-uat; cluster B hosts only production.
Separate production by cluster; share non-production by namespace when cost matters.
Environment topology
D4
Red Hat OpenShift
A regulated firm wants UAT to be a faithful rehearsal of production changes, including OpenShift and CP4I operator upgrades. Which topology BEST supports this?
A dedicated pre-production (UAT/staging) cluster configured like production (same OpenShift version, operators, storage classes and topology), separate from development and from production
UAT as a namespace inside the production cluster
UAT on developer laptops
UAT in the development namespace

Cluster-scoped changes can only be rehearsed faithfully on a cluster that mirrors production. A staging cluster with matching versions, storage and topology lets upgrades be validated before they reach production.
Correct: a production-like staging cluster supports realistic rehearsal.
Wrong: upgrading operators for UAT would also affect production.
Wrong: not representative.
Wrong: not production-like.
Every OpenShift and CP4I upgrade runs first on the staging cluster, with automated regression tests, before the production window.
'Faithful rehearsal of upgrades' points to a separate production-like cluster.
Environment topology
S3
Red Hat OpenShift
Which TWO considerations favour multi-cluster CP4I architecture over a single cluster? (Select TWO.)
Disaster recovery across regions or data centers
Isolation of production from cluster-scoped changes in non-production
Reducing the number of OpenShift clusters to administer
Avoiding the need for any replication technology

Multiple clusters enable DR (a second region) and isolate cluster-scoped change. They increase administration effort and need replication (MQ, Kafka geo-replication, API Connect 2DCDR) for data and configuration.
Correct: DR across sites needs multiple clusters.
Correct: isolation of cluster-scoped changes.
Wrong: multi-cluster increases administration.
Wrong: multi-cluster usually requires replication.
Active cluster in Frankfurt and standby in Amsterdam, with MQ and Kafka replication between them.
Multi-cluster gives isolation and DR but costs complexity. Know both sides.
Environment topology
S2
Red Hat OpenShift
When is a single OpenShift cluster with multiple availability zones (a stretched cluster within one region) appropriate for CP4I production?
When zone-level high availability is required within one region and inter-zone latency is low enough for etcd and replicated workloads
When protection against a full regional disaster is required
When zones are on different continents
Never; zones cannot be used
Multi-zone clusters survive the failure of one zone (data center) in a region with low-latency links. They do not protect against a regional outage; that needs a second cluster in another region.
Correct: multi-zone HA within a low-latency region.
Wrong: regional DR needs a separate cluster.
Wrong: etcd and replication need low latency, not intercontinental links.
Wrong: multi-zone clusters are common.
A cluster spans 3 AZs in eu-west-1; a second cluster in eu-central-1 provides DR.
HA (zones) versus DR (regions): separate concepts, separate designs.
Air-gapped installation
F1
Cloud Pak for Integration
What is an air-gapped (disconnected) installation of CP4I?
An installation where the cluster has no direct internet access, so images and catalogs are mirrored to a private registry reachable by the cluster
An installation without any storage
An installation that uses only HTTP without TLS
An installation that runs only in public cloud

Disconnected clusters cannot reach cp.icr.io. Images and catalog content are mirrored to an internal registry, using a bastion host or portable storage, and the cluster is configured to pull from the mirror.
Correct: mirror images and catalogs to a private registry.
Wrong: storage is still needed.
Wrong: TLS is still used.
Wrong: air-gapped clusters are usually on premises.
A defence ministry installs CP4I in a classified network using a bastion that mirrors images to an internal registry.
Air gap = mirror + redirect + pinned catalogs.
Air-gapped installation
S3
Red Hat OpenShift
In an air-gapped CP4I installation, which OpenShift resource redirects image pulls from cp.icr.io to the internal mirror registry without changing the image references in the operators?
ImageContentSourcePolicy, or ImageDigestMirrorSet/ImageTagMirrorSet on newer OpenShift versions
Route
NetworkPolicy
PodDisruptionBudget

Mirror policies configure CRI-O on the nodes to fetch images by digest from the mirror whenever a pod references the source registry. On OpenShift 4.13 and later, ImageDigestMirrorSet replaces the deprecated ImageContentSourcePolicy.
Correct: mirror policy resources redirect pulls.
Wrong: Routes expose services.
Wrong: NetworkPolicies control pod traffic.
Wrong: PDBs control disruption.
After applying the generated ImageDigestMirrorSet, pods referencing cp.icr.io/cp/ibm-mqadvanced-server-integration pull from registry.corp.local.
Version detail: ICSP (older) versus IDMS/ITMS (OpenShift 4.13 and later).
Air-gapped installation
T3
Red Hat OpenShift
In a disconnected cluster, a new MQ pod is in ImagePullBackOff with 'manifest unknown' from the mirror registry. Other CP4I images pull fine. What is the MOST likely cause?
That image or digest was not mirrored (for example the CASE version used for mirroring did not include this operand version)
The entitlement key is expired
The PVC is RWX
The mirror policy is not needed

'Manifest unknown' means the registry has no such image or digest. Typically the mirroring step omitted that version, for example after upgrading spec.version without re-mirroring the new CASE contents.
Correct: the image is missing from the mirror.
Wrong: in a disconnected install, pulls go to the mirror, which is a separate authentication path.
Wrong: storage is unrelated.
Wrong: the redirect is working, so the request reached the mirror.
Re-running oc ibm-pak for the new MQ CASE version and mirroring again fixed the pull.
Air-gap upgrades: mirror the new version first, then change spec.version.
Air-gapped installation
S3
Cloud Pak for Integration
Why should CatalogSources in production (especially air-gapped) installations reference catalog images by digest or a pinned version?
So operator versions are predictable and do not change unexpectedly when a floating catalog tag is updated
Because tags are not supported by OpenShift
To reduce storage costs
To disable OLM
Pinned catalogs make the available operator versions deterministic. A floating 'latest' catalog can introduce new versions automatically and trigger unplanned upgrades when approval is Automatic.
Correct: pinning ensures predictability and change control.
Wrong: tags work, but they move.
Wrong: unrelated to storage.
Wrong: OLM still manages operators.
The team upgrades catalogs deliberately as a change, never implicitly.
Predictable change: pinned catalogs plus Manual install plan approval.
Air-gapped installation
D4
Cloud Pak for Integration
An air-gapped environment has no network path at all between the internet-connected bastion and the cluster's registry. How should images be transferred?

Mirror images to portable storage (filesystem) on the connected side, physically transfer the media, then push from the filesystem into the internal registry before applying the mirror policies and catalog sources
Temporarily connect the cluster to the internet
Build images from source inside the cluster
Disable image signature and digest verification
Fully disconnected environments use a mirror-to-disk then disk-to-registry approach (for example oc image mirror or oc-mirror with a file target). This keeps digests intact and the network separate.
Correct: two-phase mirroring through portable media.
Wrong: breaks the air gap and violates policy.
Wrong: IBM images are delivered as images.
Wrong: removes supply-chain protections.
Security officers scan the transferred media before it is imported into the classified registry.
Partially disconnected -> bastion mirror. Fully disconnected -> mirror to disk and carry.
Container image registries
F2
Red Hat OpenShift
What is the role of the OpenShift internal image registry for CP4I?
It can store images built in-cluster (for example custom ACE images built by pipelines); CP4I product images are typically pulled from the IBM registry or an enterprise mirror
It is required to store all IBM product images
It stores etcd backups
It replaces cert-manager
The internal registry is useful for images built in the cluster. Product images come from cp.icr.io or a mirror. Many enterprises use an external registry (Quay, Artifactory) for both.
Correct: it suits in-cluster builds; product images come from IBM or a mirror.
Wrong: not required for IBM images.
Wrong: etcd backups go to files or object storage.
Wrong: unrelated to certificates.
A Tekton pipeline pushes custom-ace:1.4.2 to the internal registry for deployment to the dev namespace.
Know where each image comes from: product image, mirror, or custom build.
Container image registries
S3
App Connect Enterprise
A team builds custom ACE images containing BARs. Which practice is MOST appropriate for promotion across environments?
Build once, tag immutably (for example by digest), scan, sign, and promote the same image through dev, test and production
Rebuild the image separately in each environment
Use the 'latest' tag everywhere
Store images only on developers' machines
Build-once-promote-many ensures that what was tested is exactly what runs in production. Digest pinning, scanning and signing strengthen supply-chain integrity.
Correct: an immutable, scanned, signed, promoted artifact.
Wrong: rebuilding risks drift between environments.
Wrong: 'latest' is mutable and unpredictable.
Wrong: not shareable or controlled.
Production deploys image@sha256:ab12... that passed UAT, not a rebuilt one.
Build once, deploy many, pinned by digest.
Container image registries
T2
Red Hat OpenShift
Pods fail with 'x509: certificate signed by unknown authority' when pulling from an internal registry. What should be configured?
Add the registry's CA certificate to OpenShift's trusted CAs (for example additionalTrustedCA in image.config.openshift.io)
Disable all TLS
Increase pod memory
Change the PVC access mode
Nodes must trust the CA that signed the registry certificate. OpenShift supports adding trusted registry CAs through the cluster image configuration.
Correct: trust the registry's CA.
Wrong: insecure and not recommended.
Wrong: unrelated.
Wrong: unrelated.
A ConfigMap containing the corporate root CA is referenced in image.config.openshift.io/cluster under additionalTrustedCA.
x509 unknown authority -> trust chain configuration, not credentials.
Workload placement
F1
Kubernetes
What does a node taint combined with a pod toleration achieve?
A taint repels pods from a node unless the pods have a matching toleration, which enables dedicated nodes
It encrypts pod traffic
It allocates storage
It sets CPU limits
Taints mark nodes so that only pods tolerating the taint can schedule there. Combined with node affinity, they dedicate nodes to particular workloads.
Correct: taints repel; tolerations allow.
Wrong: no encryption function.
Wrong: no storage function.
Wrong: limits are set on containers.
Nodes tainted dedicated=mq:NoSchedule run only MQ pods that carry the matching toleration.
Tolerations allow placement but do not force it. Add node affinity to attract pods.
Workload placement
S3
Kubernetes
An architect wants MQ queue managers to run ONLY on a dedicated node pool and wants no other workloads on those nodes. What is the correct combination?
Taint the dedicated nodes and give MQ pods a matching toleration plus node affinity (or a nodeSelector) for those nodes
Only add a toleration to MQ pods
Only label the nodes
Set a higher priority class

A taint keeps other pods away. A toleration alone allows MQ pods there but does not force them there; affinity or a nodeSelector attracts MQ pods to those nodes. Both are needed for exclusive dedicated placement.
Correct: taint, toleration and affinity together give exclusive placement.
Wrong: tolerations do not attract pods.
Wrong: labels without taints do not keep other pods away.
Wrong: priority affects preemption, not placement.
MQ nodes carry label workload=mq and taint workload=mq:NoSchedule; QueueManager pods specify both affinity and toleration.
Dedicated nodes = taint (repel others) + affinity (attract mine).
Workload placement
S3
Kubernetes
How should replicas of an HA workload, such as three MQ Native HA pods, be spread to survive a zone failure?
Use pod anti-affinity or topologySpreadConstraints keyed on topology.kubernetes.io/zone so the replicas land in different zones
Use a nodeSelector for a single node
Run all replicas on control plane nodes
Use a DaemonSet
Spreading replicas across zones ensures that losing one zone leaves the others running. Anti-affinity or topology spread constraints on the zone label enforce this.
Correct: zone spreading through anti-affinity or spread constraints.
Wrong: a single node is a single point of failure.
Wrong: inappropriate placement.
Wrong: DaemonSets do not fit stateful queue manager replicas.
Native HA pods qm-0, qm-1 and qm-2 run in zones a, b and c.
Same zone for all replicas = correlated failure risk.
Workload placement
T3
Kubernetes
Three Event Streams broker pods use required pod anti-affinity by zone, but the cluster has worker nodes in only two zones. What happens?
The third broker pod stays Pending because no node satisfies the required anti-affinity
The scheduler ignores the rule automatically
All three pods run in one zone
The cluster adds a zone automatically
Required (hard) anti-affinity rules are never relaxed. With only two zones, the third pod cannot be placed and stays Pending. Use preferred rules or add a zone.
Correct: hard rules leave the pod unschedulable.
Wrong: required rules are not ignored.
Wrong: that would violate the rule.
Wrong: Kubernetes does not create zones.
The event message reads: 0/6 nodes are available: 6 node(s) didn't match pod anti-affinity rules.
Required affinity = guarantee or Pending. Preferred = best effort.
Workload placement
S2
Kubernetes
What is the effect of a PodDisruptionBudget (PDB) with minAvailable: 2 on a 3-replica deployment?
Voluntary disruptions such as node drains for upgrades will evict at most one pod at a time, keeping at least two available
It prevents any pod from crashing
It limits CPU usage
It sets the number of replicas
PDBs constrain voluntary evictions (drains, upgrades), not involuntary failures. They keep a minimum number of pods available during maintenance.
Correct: it limits voluntary evictions.
Wrong: crashes are involuntary.
Wrong: unrelated to CPU.
Wrong: replicas are set by the controller.
During OpenShift node upgrades, drains wait until a replacement pod is ready before evicting the next.
PDB = maintenance safety. Too strict a PDB can block node drains.
Workload placement
T3
Red Hat OpenShift

An OpenShift upgrade is stuck because a node cannot be drained. Events show 'Cannot evict pod as it would violate the pod's disruption budget'. The deployment has 1 replica and a PDB with minAvailable: 1. What is the BEST fix?
Increase replicas so the PDB can be satisfied during eviction, or adjust the PDB to match the replica count, following the workload's HA design
Delete the node
Force-kill etcd
Disable the upgrade permanently
A PDB with minAvailable equal to the replica count makes eviction impossible. Run at least 2 replicas for workloads that must stay available, or set the PDB so one pod can be disrupted.
Correct: align replicas and PDB so drains can proceed.
Wrong: destructive.
Wrong: very dangerous.
Wrong: avoids the problem rather than fixing it.
Scaling the integration runtime to 2 replicas let the drain proceed with no downtime.
PDB minAvailable equal to replicas blocks drains. Classic upgrade blocker.
Resource management
F1
Kubernetes
What is the difference between a container's resource request and its limit?
The request is what the scheduler reserves for placement; the limit is the maximum the container may use
They are identical
The limit is used for scheduling; the request is ignored
Requests apply only to storage
Requests determine scheduling and guaranteed share. Limits cap usage: CPU is throttled at the limit, and memory over the limit causes OOMKill.
Correct: request = scheduling reservation; limit = cap.
Wrong: they serve different purposes.
Wrong: the scheduler uses requests.
Wrong: they apply to CPU and memory.
An ACE runtime requests 300m CPU and 512Mi but is limited to 1 CPU and 1Gi.
Scheduling looks at requests; throttling and OOM look at limits.
Resource management
S2
Kubernetes
Which Quality of Service class does a pod get when every container's requests equal its limits for both CPU and memory?
Guaranteed
Burstable
BestEffort
Critical
Guaranteed QoS needs requests equal to limits for all containers. Such pods are the last to be evicted under node memory pressure.
Correct: equal requests and limits give Guaranteed.
Wrong: Burstable has requests lower than limits or only some set.
Wrong: BestEffort has no requests or limits.
Wrong: not a Kubernetes QoS class.
Production queue managers run as Guaranteed to minimize eviction risk.
Guaranteed = requests equal limits. Use it for critical stateful workloads.
Resource management
T3
App Connect Enterprise
An ACE integration runtime has high response times while CPU usage looks flat at exactly its limit, and the container_cpu_cfs_throttled metrics are rising. What is happening?
The container is CPU-throttled at its limit; raise the CPU limit or scale out replicas
The pod is out of memory
The PVC is full
DNS resolution is failing
When a container reaches its CPU limit, the CFS quota throttles it, which adds latency. Throttling metrics confirm this. Raise the limit (with licensing in mind) or scale horizontally.
Correct: CPU throttling at the limit.
Wrong: memory issues show as OOMKills.
Wrong: a full disk shows as write errors.
Wrong: DNS issues show as connection errors.
Doubling replicas from 2 to 4 brought p95 latency from 900 ms down to 200 ms.
Flat CPU at the limit plus latency -> throttling.
Resource management
S3
Kubernetes
Which approach sets sensible defaults for containers that developers deploy without specifying requests or limits?
A LimitRange in the namespace with default requests and limits
A ResourceQuota alone
A NetworkPolicy
A Route annotation

LimitRange applies default requests and limits (and enforces min and max values) for containers that do not specify them. A ResourceQuota on compute resources actually requires pods to specify requests and limits, so the two work together.
Correct: LimitRange supplies defaults.
Wrong: quota caps totals and can reject pods without resource settings.
Wrong: unrelated.
Wrong: unrelated.
The dev namespace defaults containers to 100m/256Mi requests and 500m/512Mi limits.
Quota without LimitRange defaults can cause 'must specify limits' rejections.
Resource management
D4
Cloud Pak for Integration
An architect must set CPU requests and limits for production MQ, ACE and Kafka workloads, balancing performance, licensing and stability. Which strategy is BEST?

Set requests from measured steady-state usage, set limits from tested peak needs (remembering that limits drive licensed VPC), use Guaranteed QoS for critical stateful components, and review regularly with monitoring data
Set very high limits on everything to avoid throttling
Set no limits so the cluster self-balances
Copy development values to production
Data-driven sizing balances cost and performance. Because licensed VPCs are based on limits, limits must be deliberate. Critical stateful systems benefit from Guaranteed QoS.
Correct: a measured, licensing-aware, QoS-aware approach.
Wrong: inflates license usage and wastes capacity.
Wrong: unpredictable and can inflate license measurement.
Wrong: development is not representative of production load.
After load testing, the Kafka brokers get 4 CPU limits and requests (Guaranteed), and ACE runtimes get 1 CPU request and 2 CPU limit.
Limits matter twice: performance (throttling) and licensing.
Operators and OLM
F1
Operator Lifecycle Manager
Which OLM object expresses the intent to install an operator from a catalog and keep it updated on a channel?
Subscription
PersistentVolumeClaim

Broker advertised listeners or per-broker routes are not reachable from the client network (for example firewall or DNS for the per-broker route hostnames)
Topic retention is too short
The consumer group is wrong
The schema registry is down

Kafka clients first contact the bootstrap address, then connect directly to each broker's advertised address. With external route listeners, each broker has its own route hostname, which must resolve and be reachable.
Correct: per-broker addresses must be reachable.
Wrong: unrelated to connectivity.
Wrong: unrelated.
